subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Wuyi Rock Tea
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Wuyi Rock Tea.

hook.text: Wuyi Mountain teas are called 'rock teas' because the plants grow in crevices between ancient sandstone cliffs.

buildup.text: Thin, mineral-rich soil forces deep root systems. Mist and shade from canyon walls protect the delicate leaves.

discovery.text: The result is 'yan yun'—rock rhyme—a mineral taste sensation unique to Wuyi teas that lingers in the mouth.

twist.text: Da Hong Pao (Big Red Robe) from the original six bushes is the most expensive tea ever sold—over $1M per kilogram.

climax.text: Those original bushes are now government-protected. All commercial Da Hong Pao comes from cuttings and grafts.

punchline.text: Rock, mist, centuries of roots. Wuyi teas taste like geology.

quiz.question: What is 'yan yun' in Wuyi rock teas?
options: A mineral taste sensation unique to rock-grown teas

details.summary: Wuyi rock teas, or yancha, grow in the stony cliffs and narrow valleys of Wuyi Mountain in Fujian. The mineral-rich rocky soil imparts a distinctive taste called yanyun, or rock rhyme. Da Hong Pao is the most famous variety, and authentic examples rank among the most expensive teas in the world.
details.whyItMatters: Wuyi rock tea is where terroir matters most in the tea world. The rocky growing environment creates flavors no other region can replicate.
takeaways: Yancha grows in rocky cliffs of Wuyi Mountain, Fujian
Mineral-rich soil creates the unique rock rhyme flavor
Da Hong Pao is the most famous and expensive variety

faq.question: What is rock rhyme in Wuyi tea?
faq.answer: Yanyun, or rock rhyme, describes the mineral backbone and lingering mouthfeel unique to teas grown in Wuyi's rocky terrain. It is a combination of minerality, body, and a persistent aftertaste that distinguishes true rock tea from oolongs grown in flat farmland elsewhere.

faq.question: Why is Da Hong Pao so expensive?
faq.answer: Original Da Hong Pao comes from a few ancient mother trees on a Wuyi cliff, now protected and no longer harvested. Modern Da Hong Pao is produced from cuttings of these trees. Premium versions from core Wuyi zones still sell for thousands of dollars per kilogram due to limited supply.
